---
title: "Missing genotypes: impute only when you must"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  dpi = 100
)
```

Most datasets have missing genotypes, and many tools ask for them to be
imputed first. Simple imputation (e.g. with the most common genotype of each
locus) is fast, but it is not neutral: an individual with many missing
genotypes receives many copies of the same, typical genotypes, which pull it
towards the centre of the data and make the individuals with much missing
data look alike. Missingness then becomes a signal of its own.

`tidypopgen` avoids this where it can. The default PCA, `gt_pca()`, compares
each pair of individuals over the loci genotyped in both (as `plink --pca`
does). `gt_dapc()` and `gt_pcadapt()` work on that PCA: DAPC estimates the
loadings of each locus over the individuals genotyped at it, and pcadapt
tests each locus on the individuals genotyped at it. LD clumping
(`loci_ld_clump()`) and pruning (`loci_ld_prune()`) compute the correlation
between two loci over the individuals genotyped at both, as PLINK does.
Imputation is only needed by the methods that require complete genotypes,
such as `gt_pca(method = "random")` (for very large numbers of individuals)
and `gt_pca_autoSVD()`.

This article compares the two approaches on simulated data, where we know
the truth.

## Simulated data

We simulate 4 populations of 50 individuals with the Balding-Nichols model
(`gt_simulate_bn()`): 5,000 neutral loci (F~ST~ = 0.05), and 100 outlier
loci strongly differentiated in the first population (F~ST~ = 0.7 in that
population), as loci under selection would be. Each individual misses a proportion of its genotypes,
from 0 to 80% (as is common, e.g., with ancient DNA), at random loci. Since
`gt_simulate_bn()` draws the genotypes before the missing ones, the same
seeds give the complete data, our truth. We group each `gen_tibble` by
population as soon as we create it.

```{r simulate}
library(tidypopgen)
library(ggplot2)

n_indiv <- rep(50, 4)
set.seed(42)
missing_rate <- runif(sum(n_indiv), 0, 0.8)

simulate_data <- function(missing) {
  set.seed(1)
  neutral <- gt_simulate_bn(
    n_indiv = n_indiv, n_loci = 5000, fst = 0.05, missing = missing
  )
  set.seed(2)
  outliers <- gt_simulate_bn(
    n_indiv = n_indiv, n_loci = 100, fst = c(0.7, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05),
    missing = missing
  )
  gen_tibble(
    x = cbind(show_genotypes(neutral), show_genotypes(outliers)),
    indiv_meta = data.frame(id = neutral$id, population = neutral$population),
    loci = data.frame(
      name = c(paste0("neutral", 1:5000), paste0("outlier", 1:100)),
      chromosome = "1", position = 1:5100 * 1000L, genetic_dist = 0,
      allele_ref = "A", allele_alt = "G"
    ),
    backingfile = tempfile(), quiet = TRUE
  )
}
complete_gt <- simulate_data(missing = 0) %>%
  group_by(population)
missing_gt <- simulate_data(missing = missing_rate) %>%
  group_by(population)

# keep the loci that are polymorphic in the data with missing genotypes
polymorphic <- loci_names(missing_gt)[loci_maf(missing_gt$genotypes) > 0]
complete_gt <- complete_gt %>% select_loci(all_of(polymorphic))
missing_gt <- missing_gt %>% select_loci(all_of(polymorphic))
outlier <- startsWith(polymorphic, "outlier")
missing_gt
```

We also impute the missing genotypes, with the most common genotype of each
locus. The imputed genotypes are stored alongside the original ones, and are
only used when we ask for them, with `gt_set_imputed()`:

```{r impute}
missing_gt <- gt_impute_simple(missing_gt, method = "mode")
```

## PCA

We run three PCAs: of the complete genotypes (the truth), of the genotypes
with missing values (compared pairwise, without imputation), and of the
imputed genotypes.

```{r pca}
pca_complete <- gt_pca(complete_gt, k = 5)
pca_missing <- gt_pca(missing_gt, k = 5)
gt_set_imputed(missing_gt, set = TRUE)
pca_imputed <- gt_pca(missing_gt, k = 5)
gt_set_imputed(missing_gt, set = FALSE)
pca_missing
```

To compare them, we plot the first two components of each PCA (with their
signs matched to those of the truth), and colour the individuals by
population, with larger points for those with more missing genotypes:

```{r pca_plot, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Scores of the first two principal components of the complete data, of the data with missing genotypes, and of the imputed data"}
# the scores of the first k components, with their signs matched to the
# complete data
matched_scores <- function(pca, k = 3) {
  u <- pca$u[, 1:k]
  sweep(u, 2, sign(diag(stats::cor(u, pca_complete$u[, 1:k]))), "*")
}
pcas <- list(
  complete = pca_complete, missing = pca_missing, imputed = pca_imputed
)
scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pcas), function(method) {
  u <- matched_scores(pcas[[method]])
  data.frame(
    method = method, population = missing_gt$population,
    missing = indiv_missingness(missing_gt), PC1 = u[, 1], PC2 = u[, 2]
  )
}))
scores$method <- factor(scores$method, levels = names(pcas))
ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = population, size = missing)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.5, 3)) +
  labs(size = "missing\ngenotypes") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The PCA of the genotypes with missing values recovers the populations of the
complete data, however many genotypes an individual misses. With imputation,
the individuals with many missing genotypes are drawn together, whatever
their population, and the first component orders the individuals by their
missing genotypes rather than by population. The correlations of the
components with those of the truth, and with the proportion of missing
genotypes of each individual, show it:

```{r pca_cor}
pc_cor <- function(pca) {
  u <- matched_scores(pca)
  c(
    stats::setNames(
      abs(diag(stats::cor(u, pca_complete$u[, 1:3]))),
      paste("truth, PC", 1:3)
    ),
    stats::setNames(
      abs(stats::cor(u, indiv_missingness(missing_gt)))[, 1],
      paste("missingness, PC", 1:3)
    )
  )
}
round(sapply(pcas[-1], pc_cor), 2)
```

## DAPC

We run a DAPC on each PCA, with the populations as groups. With a PCA of
missing genotypes, `gt_dapc()` needs the `gen_tibble` (`data`) to estimate
the loadings of the loci over the individuals genotyped at each of them; loci
with more than half of their genotypes missing (`max_missing`) get `NA`
loadings, as, estimated from few individuals, they would be noisy:

```{r dapc}
pops <- as.factor(missing_gt$population)
dapc_complete <- gt_dapc(pca_complete, pop = pops, n_pca = 3)
dapc_missing <- gt_dapc(pca_missing, pop = pops, n_pca = 3, data = missing_gt)
dapc_imputed <- gt_dapc(pca_imputed, pop = pops, n_pca = 3)
```

We compare the proportion of individuals assigned to their population, the
number of outlier loci among the 100 loci that contribute most to the
discriminant functions (summed over the axes), and the rank correlation of
these contributions with those of the complete data:

```{r dapc_compare}
dapcs <- list(
  complete = dapc_complete, missing = dapc_missing, imputed = dapc_imputed
)
top_outliers <- function(stat, n = 100) sum(outlier[order(-stat)[1:n]])
contribution <- function(x) rowSums(x$var.contr, na.rm = TRUE)
round(sapply(dapcs, function(x) {
  c(
    "correctly assigned" = mean(x$assign == pops),
    "outliers in top 100 loci" = top_outliers(contribution(x)),
    "correlation with complete" = stats::cor(contribution(x),
      contribution(dapc_complete),
      method = "spearman"
    )
  )
}), 2)
```

Without imputation, the DAPC assigns the individuals as it does with the
complete data, and the contributions of the loci are close to those of the
complete data. With imputation, some individuals with many missing
genotypes are assigned to the wrong population, and fewer outliers stand
out.

In the contributions of the loci (summed over the discriminant axes), the
outlier loci (the last 100) stand out in all three analyses, but those of the
data with missing genotypes look most like those of the complete data; with
imputation, more neutral loci reach high contributions:

```{r dapc_contributions, fig.alt = "Contributions of the loci to the discriminant functions, for the DAPC of the complete data, of the data with missing genotypes, and of the imputed data"}
contributions <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(dapcs), function(method) {
  data.frame(
    method = method, locus = seq_along(outlier),
    contribution = contribution(dapcs[[method]]), outlier = outlier
  )
}))
contributions$method <- factor(contributions$method, levels = names(dapcs))
ggplot(contributions, aes(locus, contribution, colour = outlier)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  labs(y = "contribution to the\ndiscriminant functions") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## pcadapt

Finally, we scan for outlier loci with pcadapt, on 3 components of each PCA.
With the PCA of missing genotypes, `gt_pcadapt()` tests each locus on the
individuals genotyped at it; with the PCA of imputed genotypes, it uses the
imputed genotypes:

```{r pcadapt}
pcadapt_complete <- gt_pcadapt(complete_gt, pca_complete, k = 3)
pcadapt_missing <- gt_pcadapt(missing_gt, pca_missing, k = 3)
pcadapt_imputed <- gt_pcadapt(missing_gt, pca_imputed, k = 3)
pcadapts <- list(
  complete = pcadapt_complete, missing = pcadapt_missing,
  imputed = pcadapt_imputed
)
round(sapply(pcadapts, function(x) {
  c(
    "outliers in top 100 loci" = top_outliers(x$score),
    "correlation with complete" = stats::cor(x$score, pcadapt_complete$score,
      method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"
    )
  )
}), 2)
```

Without imputation, pcadapt finds almost as many outliers as with the
complete data, and ranks the loci much as the complete data do (the
`r sum(is.na(pcadapt_missing$score))` loci with more than half of their
genotypes missing are not tested, as with `gt_dapc()`, and are left out of
the correlation). With
imputation, one of the components that pcadapt uses reflects missingness
rather than populations, and fewer outliers are found.

## When to impute

Use the genotypes with their missing values whenever the analysis can: the
default `gt_pca()` (and `pairwise_grm(method = "plink")`), `gt_dapc()`,
`gt_pcadapt()`, `predict()` of a PCA (least squares projection),
`loci_ld_clump()` and `loci_ld_prune()`, and the `pairwise_*()`,
`indiv_*()`, `loci_*()` and `pop_*()` statistics.

Impute (e.g. with
`gt_impute_simple()`, and `gt_set_imputed()` to use the imputed genotypes)
only for the methods that need complete data, such as
`gt_pca(method = "random")` and `gt_pca_autoSVD()`; those functions say so if
they find missing genotypes.
